answer: Menuschool's submission is honest and well-structured, but it reads as a promising student project more than a venture case. Priority improvements: (1) Replace vague quantities with verified numbers. 'Several hundred programs,' 'a few thousand dollars,' and 'several hundred dollars per seat' should become sourced figures (e.g., NCES/IPEDS data, ACF accreditation lists, state CTE directories) with an explicit bottom-up TAM/SAM/SOM, seats x price. Do the math on the page so a reader can check it. (2) Show evidence of willingness to pay, not just interest. Positive feedback and time-savings anecdotes from ~40 students at two programs are weak validation. Convert pilots into signed LOIs, paid pilots at a nominal fee, or pre-orders, and report how many instructors interviewed, what they said about price, and who controls the budget. Quote specific instructors or chefs (with permission). (3) Sharpen the answer to the central risk: 'why not a spreadsheet?' Quantify the time saved (e.g., hours to build a costed lesson plan manually vs. in Menuschool) and show a before/after example. Include learning-outcome evidence if any (did students understand food cost better?). (4) Address the market-size question directly rather than only asking for feedback. A low-single-digit-million U.S. market is a lifestyle business or feature, not a venture-scale company. Make a clear thesis: either a credible expansion path with sizing (hospitality management programs, corporate training, continuing ed, international) or a deliberate positioning as a sustainable niche business or an acquirable feature. Indecision reads as a lack of strategy. (5) Strengthen the go-to-market and sales-cycle plan. Public institution procurement is slow; explain how you will navigate it (pilot-to-purchase pathways, purchase-order thresholds, Perkins/CTE funding, consortium or state contracts, textbook-publisher or association partnerships) and give a realistic timeline for the target of five paying programs. (6) Tighten the competitive and defensibility analysis. Name specific competitors (restaurant costing tools, existing culinary education platforms, LMS integrations, publisher digital products) and explain why an incumbent adding an 'education mode' would be slow or unlikely. Articulate moats: curated recipe/lesson library, pricing data integrations, instructor network, switching costs from converted recipe libraries. (7) De-risk the data dependency. Pricing data is core to the product but its source and cost are 'still being evaluated.' Identify candidate sources, their costs, update frequency, and regional coverage, and show how this affects margins. Address the regional-pricing feedback you already received. (8) Build out the financials. Provide unit economics (price per seat, conversion service margin, data cost per program, support cost), a simple 12-18 month budget tied to the funding ask, and the milestones the money unlocks. Specify the amount requested and how each dollar maps to a measurable outcome (e.g., X paid pilots, Y conversion rate). (9) Clarify the business model focus. Software licenses plus conversion services plus consulting is three businesses; explain which is primary, how services support rather than distract from software scaling, and whether services are a wedge or a margin drag. (10) Strengthen the team section. Add the industry or edtech advisor (or name the candidates and what they would provide), and explicitly cover gaps: sales experience with institutions, product/data engineering depth, and post-graduation commitment of all three founders. (11) Close with a clear milestone roadmap and risk list: legal formation, first paid contract, pricing data deal, retention evidence, with dates. Overall, the writing is clear and candid, which is a strength; the fix is converting estimates and hopes into evidence, numbers, and a decisive strategic position.
